newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China powerhouses emerge in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: China powerhouses emerge in Hong Kong.

text.p: Chinese conglomerates are emerging as the new powerhouses of Hong Kong's corporate scene, ready to take on the mantle of the old "hongs" who dominated the territory during British colonial rule.
A dramatic shift in the landscape is under way as Britain prepares to hand Hong Kong back to China next July 1.
"The whole picture in Hong Kong is changing," said Ching-ju Yeh, senior investment manager at HSBC Asset Management.
"The impression is that for some of the traditional old names, the influence will start to decline and new names from China are getting a much higher profile," she said.

Changes in Hong Kong's business environment have already been anticipated by investors and China-related shares have been snapped up eagerly this year on expectations these firms will flourish when Hong Kong becomes their home turf.

"Institutional investors are hedging themselves against a drop in influence from the British-related companies, which were the historical landlords of Hong Kong, and increasing their weightings in red chips," said Charles de Trenck, senior analyst at Kerry Securities.
"There is a re-rating of China-related shares because of the handover. The red chips that have diversified portfolios and reasonable management are being targeted as future hongs."
Red chips are firms with financial backing from China.
Some of Hong Kong's hongs -- the old name for large trading houses -- go back to the founding of the British colony in the mid-19th century.
Names such as Jardine Matheson & Co, Butterfield and Swire, Wheelock Marden and Hutchison Whampoa wielded great influence in the affairs of Hong Kong.

But the territory will be handed back to China at midnight on June 30, 1997 and the return to Chinese sovereignty will allow the rise of companies like CITIC Pacific Ltd, Guangdong Investment Ltd, China Resources Enterprise Ltd and Shanghai Industrial, analysts said.
"The companies with Chinese background or capital want to replace the status of the British conglomerates," said Chen Man Lung, senior analyst at China Everbright Research Limited.
HG Asia said in a recent report there are currently about 2,000 China-backed companies in Hong Kong with an estimated US$42.5 billion investment in the local economy.

"Given the much stronger investment environment of Hong Kong compared with other mainland cities, these companies are likely to compete for the economic advantages currently enjoyed by the established players," it said.
"CITIC Pacific and Guangdong Investment are likely to emerge as influential conglomerates in the territory post 1997."
Analysts said the rapid rise of these China-backed firms is likely to be boosted by valuable asset injections by influential state-owned parents.
Although it is hard to say just how wealthy the parents are, they said backing from a provincial government assures financial support and access to important business.

"Some of the influential concept stocks like Guangdong Investment and Shanghai Industrial will definitely emerge. These two stocks represent the most influential provinces in the southeast," said Morgan Stanley's China analyst Jason Cheung.
"When China controls Hong Kong after 1997, a lot of favour will be granted to these types of enterprises. Those guys that do not have the right connections will fall," he said.
CITIC Pacific, the Hong Kong branch of Beijing's official foreign trading arm China International Trust and Investment Corp, has become a role model for emerging Chinese firms.
The company has already ascended to blue chip status and its assets have swelled through acquisitions and asset injections.
Other companies are expected to follow suit and Guangdong Investment, also a blue chip, is well on its way.
Controlled by Guangdong province, Guangdong Investment engages in investment holding, hotel ownership and management. Its shares are up about 18 percent this year.

"These companies grow by injection so they acquire and they grow, they raise funds and they acquire and they grow," said de Trenck. "You don't see the hongs issue shares in the same way. You do see them selling down stakes. You don't see them acquiring new assets."

China Resources is controlled by China's Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation and has a wide array of businesses ranging from brewing to property to cold storage. Its shares have risen about 74 percent this year.
"It's being regarded as a conglomerate in the making. They have a very diversified portfolio," said Chen.

Investors have also singled out Shanghai Industrial as a promising performer. A newcomer to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, its shares have risen about 88 percent since the company launched an initial public offering in May this year.

The firm is an investment arm of the Shanghai municipal government and makes cigarettes, pharmaceuticals, personal care, packaging and printing products. It plans to invest in other consumer product firms as well as the automotive industry, telecommunications and bio-pharmaceuticals.
"China Merchants is a perfect example of a hong because it has been around for over 100 years and has gone through so many changes and transformations," added Kerry's de Trenck.
"It has staked a few core businesses but has also been very diversified. You could compare China Merchants to a Swire."

China Merchants China Direct Investments Ltd is a closed-end investment company which invests in unlisted enterprises in manufacturing, transport and related projects, the service sector and real estate in China.
As well as rapidly growing businesses, China-related firms are also increasing their might on the Hong Kong stock market by issuing new shares and launching other fund-raising exercises.

Their presence is likely to be felt in all sectors of the economy. "I think they will be present in all sectors. In banking you have the Bank of China and in property you have China Resources and China Overseas and in the airlines we will see more coming," said Yeh.

In preparation for the handover, some British Hongs have been establishing ties with Chinese firms. "The old Hong Kong group realise they have to cooperate with China. They will start to lose some of the privileges they had before," said Yeh.

Swire Pacific Ltd has actively sought partnerships in China, teaming up with CITIC Pacific in 1985, and has invested heavily in the mainland. Its Cathay Pacific Airlines Ltd unit is also 25-percent owned by CITIC Pacific.
Jardine Matheson has 70 joint ventures in China but is content to remain a foreign firm trading in China.
Analysts said changes are likely to be gradual and much depends on the strength of China's economy.

"It is too early to say what the impact will be but you assume it will happen because they have greater access to what the central government is thinking and in future they will be much closer," said Yeh.
